claim: The gut microbiome affects host phenotypes including aiding digestion and energy uptake.
source: Host phenotypes affected by the gut microbiome are documented in humans (Ley et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009; Lynch and Pedersen, 2016), laboratory animals (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2008; Rolig et al., 2015; Rosshart et al., 2017; Gould et al., 2018), and wild populations (Suzuki, 2017; Roth et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2020a; Hua et al., 2020), and include critical traits such as aiding digestion and energy uptake (Rowland et al., 2018), and the development and regulation of the immune system (Davenport, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research documenting gut microbiome effects on host phenotypes.

claim: The gut microbiome affects the development and regulation of the immune system.
source: Host phenotypes affected by the gut microbiome are documented in humans (Ley et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2009; Lynch and Pedersen, 2016), laboratory animals (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2008; Rolig et al., 2015; Rosshart et al., 2017; Gould et al., 2018), and wild populations (Suzuki, 2017; Roth et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2020a; Hua et al., 2020), and include critical traits such as aiding digestion and energy uptake (Rowland et al., 2018), and the development and regulation of the immune system (Davenport, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on immune system development and regulation.

claim: Gut microbiome community composition varies significantly among host species, populations, and individuals.
source: Despite the importance of the gut microbiome, community composition varies significantly among host species, populations, and individuals (Benson et al., 2010; Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Brooks et al., 2016; Rehman et al., 2016; Amato et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies documenting variation in microbiome composition.

claim: Alterations of the gut microbiome are linked to diabetes.
source: While a portion of this variation is expected to be selectively neutral, alterations of the gut microbiome are on the one hand linked to numerous human diseases (Carding et al., 2015; Lynch and Pedersen, 2016), including diabetes (Qin, 2012), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Ott et al., 2004; Gevers et al., 2014), and mental disorders (Clapp et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to research linking gut microbiome alterations to diabetes.

claim: Alterations of the gut microbiome are linked to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
source: While a portion of this variation is expected to be selectively neutral, alterations of the gut microbiome are on the one hand linked to numerous human diseases (Carding et al., 2015; Lynch and Pedersen, 2016), including diabetes (Qin, 2012), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Ott et al., 2004; Gevers et al., 2014), and mental disorders (Clapp et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to research linking gut microbiome alterations to IBD.

claim: Alterations of the gut microbiome are linked to mental disorders.

evidence: Supported by citation to research linking gut microbiome alterations to mental disorders.

claim: The gut microbiome can play an important role in adaptation on recent evolutionary timescales.
source: On the other hand, there is evidence that the gut microbiome can play an important role in adaptation on both recent (Hehemann et al., 2010; Suzuki and Ley, 2020b) and ancient evolutionary timescales (Rausch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on gut microbiome role in recent adaptation.

claim: The gut microbiome can play an important role in adaptation on ancient evolutionary timescales.
source: On the other hand, there is evidence that the gut microbiome can play an important role in adaptation on both recent (Hehemann et al., 2010; Suzuki and Ley, 2020b) and ancient evolutionary timescales (Rausch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on gut microbiome role in ancient adaptation.

claim: The pattern of diversification among gut microbiomes appears to mirror host phylogeny.
source: An intriguing observation made in comparative microbiome research in the last decade is that the pattern of diversification among gut microbiomes appears to mirror host phylogeny (Ochman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to research documenting phylosymbiosis patterns.

claim: Phylosymbiosis is documented in a number of diverse host taxa.
source: This phenomenon, coined 'phylosymbiosis' (Brucker and Bordenstein, 2012a; Brucker and Bordenstein, 2012b; Lim and Bordenstein, 2020), is documented in a number of diverse host taxa (Brooks et al., 2016) and also extends to the level of the phageome (Gogarten et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to research documenting phylosymbiosis across diverse taxa.

claim: Phylosymbiosis extends to the level of the phageome.
source: This phenomenon, coined 'phylosymbiosis' (Brucker and Bordenstein, 2012a; Brucker and Bordenstein, 2012b; Lim and Bordenstein, 2020), is documented in a number of diverse host taxa (Brooks et al., 2016) and also extends to the level of the phageome (Gogarten et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on phageome phylosymbiosis.

claim: Signatures of cospeciation/codiversification are present among numerous mammalian associated gut microbes.
source: However, it is likely that vertical inheritance is important for at least a subset of taxa, as signatures of cospeciation/codiversification are present among numerous mammalian associated gut microbes (Moeller et al., 2016; Groussin et al., 2017; Moeller et al., 2019), which could also set the stage for potential coevolutionary processes.
evidence: Supported by citations to research documenting cospeciation signatures in mammalian gut microbes.

claim: Interspecific fecal microbiota transplants provide evidence of host adaptation to their conspecific microbial communities.
source: Importantly, experiments involving interspecific fecal microbiota transplants indeed provide evidence of host adaptation to their conspecific microbial communities (Brooks et al., 2016; Moeller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on fecal microbiota transplants.

claim: Cospeciating taxa were observed to be significantly enriched among the bacterial species depleted in early onset IBD.
source: Furthermore, cospeciating taxa were observed to be significantly enriched among the bacterial species depleted in early onset IBD, an immune-related disorder, suggesting a greater evolved dependency on such taxa (Papa et al., 2012; Groussin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on cospeciating taxa and IBD.

claim: Mus musculus musculus and Mus musculus domesticus share a common ancestor approximately 0.5 million years ago.
source: We previously analysed the gut microbiome across the Central European hybrid zone of Mus musculus musculus and Mus musculus domesticus (Wang et al., 2015), which share a common ancestor ~0.5 million years ago (Geraldes et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on mouse subspecies divergence time.

claim: Transgressive phenotypes among gut microbial traits were common in hybrids between M. m. musculus and M. m. domesticus.
source: Importantly, transgressive phenotypes (i.e. exceeding or falling short of parental values) among gut microbial traits as well as increased intestinal histopathology scores were common in hybrids, suggesting that the genetic basis of host control over microbes has diverged (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on hybrid mouse microbiomes.

evidence: Supported by citations to research on laboratory mouse microbiome deviations.

claim: The mucosa-associated microbiota has more direct interaction with host cells than luminal microbiota.
source: In this study, we employed a powerful genetic mapping approach using inbred lines directly derived from the M. m. musculus–M. m. domesticus hybrid zone, and further focus on the mucosa-associated microbiota due to its more direct interaction with host cells (Fukata and Arditi, 2013; Chu and Mazmanian, 2013), distinct functions compared to the luminal microbiota (Wang et al., 2010; Vaga et al., 2020), and greater dependence on host genetics (Spor et al., 2011; Linnenbrink et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on mucosa-associated microbiota characteristics.

evidence: Supported by comparison of candidate genes to human mGWAS results.

source: Subsequently, we merged the information from Mills et al., 2020 and the seven previous QTL mapping studies discussed above to further narrow down the most promising candidate genes, and found 30 genes overlapping with our study.
evidence: Supported by integration of multiple lines of evidence.

evidence: Supported by integration of multiple lines of evidence.

evidence: Supported by protein-protein interaction network analysis of curated candidate genes.

claim: GNG12 and C3 are the proteins with the most edges in the curated candidate gene network (30 and 25, respectively).

claim: MCHR1, CXCL12, and NMUR2 each have 18 edges in the curated candidate gene network.
source: The G-protein, GNG12 and the complement component 3 C3, are the proteins with the most edges in the network (30 and 25, respectively), followed by MCHR1, CXCL12, and NMUR2 with each 18 edges.
evidence: Supported by network analysis of curated candidate genes shown in Figure 6.

claim: Of the 79 highly connected genes, 35 are associated with bacteria that are either cospeciating (cospeciation rate >0.5) and/or have high heritability (>0.5).
source: Of these 79 highly connected genes, 35 are associated with bacteria that are either cospeciating (cospeciation rate >0.5; Groussin et al., 2017) and/or have high heritability (>0.5) suggesting a functionally important role for these bacterial taxa.
evidence: Supported by integration of network analysis with cospeciation and heritability data.

claim: This study is unique in using mice collected from a naturally occurring hybrid zone together with their native microbes, yielding extremely high mapping resolution.
source: First, the unique genetic resource of mice collected from a naturally occurring hybrid zone together with their native microbes yielded extremely high mapping resolution and the possibility to uncover ongoing evolutionary processes in nature.
evidence: Describes unique features of the study design.

claim: This study is the first to perform genetic mapping of 16S rRNA transcripts in the gut environment.
source: Second, our study is the first to perform genetic mapping of 16S rRNA transcripts in the gut environment, which was previously shown to be superior to DNA-based profiling in a genetic mapping study of the skin microbiota (Belheouane et al., 2017).
evidence: Describes unique features of the study design and cites previous work on RNA-based profiling.

claim: This study is one of the only to specifically examine the mucosa-associated community.
source: Third, our study is one of the only to specifically examine the mucosa-associated community.
evidence: Describes unique features of the study design.

claim: Genetic relatedness in the mapping population significantly correlates with microbiome similarity.
source: Genetic relatedness in our mapping population significantly correlates with microbiome similarity, supporting a basis for codiversification at the early stages of speciation.
evidence: Supported by analysis of genetic relatedness and microbiome similarity in this study.

claim: 14% (DNA based) to 20% (RNA based) of bacterial taxa have significant heritability estimates.
source: By performing 16S rRNA gene profiling at both the DNA and RNA level, we found that 14% (DNA based) to 20% (RNA based) of bacterial taxa have significant heritability estimates, with values up to 83%.
evidence: Supported by heritability analysis performed in this study.

claim: The proportion of heritable taxa and maximum value of heritability estimates are consistent with previous studies in humans and mice.
source: The proportion of heritable taxa and maximum value of heritability estimates are consistent with previous studies in humans and mice ( O'Connor et al., 2014; Org et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous heritability studies.

claim: Mice were raised in a controlled common environment, which likely contributes to high heritability values for some taxa.
source: First, mice were raised in a controlled common environment, and heritability estimates in other mammals were shown to be contingent on the environment (Grieneisen et al., 2021).
evidence: Describes study design and cites research on environmental effects on heritability.

claim: Bacterial communities were sampled from cecal tissue (mucosa) instead of lumen/faeces, which likely contributes to high heritability values.
source: Second, bacterial communities were sampled from cecal tissue (mucosa) instead of lumen/faeces (Linnenbrink et al., 2013).
evidence: Describes study design and cites research on mucosa-associated microbiota.

claim: Genetic variation in the mapping population was higher than in typical mapping studies due to subspecies differences, which likely contributes to high heritability values.
source: Third, genetic variation in our mapping population was higher than in typical mapping studies due to subspecies differences.
evidence: Describes study design and its implications for heritability estimates.

claim: Heritability estimates for RNA-based traits suggest that host genetic effects are more strongly reflected by bacterial activity than cell number.
source: Notably, heritability estimates for RNA-based traits are significantly correlated with previously reported cospeciation rates in mammals (Groussin et al., 2017). This pattern, as well as the higher proportion of heritable taxa for RNA-based traits, suggest that host genetic effects are more strongly reflected by bacterial activity than cell number.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between RNA-based heritability and cospeciation rates.

claim: A median of four significant loci per taxon suggests a complex and polygenic genetic architecture affecting bacterial abundances.
source: Taxa had a median of four significant loci, suggesting a complex and polygenic genetic architecture affecting bacterial abundances.
evidence: Inferred from the number of significant loci per taxon.

claim: This study identifies a higher number of loci compared to previous QTL and GWAS studies in mice.
source: We identify a higher number of loci in comparison to previous QTL and GWAS studies in mice (Benson et al., 2010; McKnite et al., 2012; Leamy et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Org et al., 2015; Snijders et al., 2016; Kemis et al., 2019), which may be due to a number of factors.
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous mapping studies.

claim: The parental strains of this study were never subjected to rederivation and subsequent reconstitution of their microbiota.
source: The parental strains of our study were never subjected to rederivation and subsequent reconstitution of their microbiota, and natural mouse gut microbiota are more variable than the artificial microbiota of laboratory strains (Kohl and Dearing, 2014; Weldon et al., 2015; Suzuki, 2017; Rosshart et al., 2017).
evidence: Describes study design and cites research on natural vs. laboratory microbiota.

claim: Natural mouse gut microbiota are more variable than the artificial microbiota of laboratory strains.
source: The parental strains of our study were never subjected to rederivation and subsequent reconstitution of their microbiota, and natural mouse gut microbiota are more variable than the artificial microbiota of laboratory strains (Kohl and Dearing, 2014; Weldon et al., 2015; Suzuki, 2017; Rosshart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on natural vs. laboratory microbiota.

claim: The mapping population harbours both within-subspecies and between-subspecies genetic variation.
source: Furthermore, as noted above, our mapping population harbours both within-subspecies and between-subspecies genetic variation.
evidence: Describes the genetic composition of the mapping population.

claim: The study may capture the effects of mutations that fixed rapidly between subspecies due to strong selection.
source: We crossed incipient species sharing a common ancestor ~0.5 million years ago, hence we may also capture the effects of mutations that fixed rapidly between subspecies due to strong selection, which are typically not variable within species (Walsh and Lynch, 1998; Barton and Keightley, 2002).
evidence: Inferred from the study design and cited research on mutation fixation.

claim: For the majority of loci, the allele associated with lower relative abundance of the bacterial taxon was (partially) dominant.
source: For the majority of loci, the allele associated with lower relative abundance of the bacterial taxon was (partially) dominant.
evidence: Supported by dominance analysis of significant loci.

claim: The dominance pattern suggests there is strong purifying selection against a high abundance of any particular taxon, which may help ensure high alpha diversity.
source: This suggests there is strong purifying selection against a high abundance of any particular taxon, which may help ensure high alpha diversity.
evidence: Inferred from the observed dominance patterns.

claim: The transgressive phenotypes observed can be explained by overdominance, underdominance, or epistasis.
source: This pattern can be explained by overdominance or underdominance, or by epistasis (Rieseberg et al., 1999).
evidence: Inferred from observed transgressive phenotypes and cited research on genetic mechanisms.

claim: Chromosome 2 169–171 Mb is associated with ASV23 (Eisenbergiella), Eisenbergiella and ASV32 (unclassified Lachnospiraceae) in this study.
source: For example, chromosome 2 169–171 Mb is associated with ASV23 (Eisenbergiella), Eisenbergiella and ASV32 (unclassified Lachnospiraceae) in this study, and overlaps with significant loci from three previous studies (Leamy et al., 2014; Snijders et al., 2016; Kemis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide association mapping results and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Chromosome 5 101–103 Mb is significantly associated with four taxa in this study (Prevotellaceae, Paraprevotella, ASV7 genus Paraprevotella and Acetatifactor).
source: Another hotspot is on chromosome 5 101–103 Mb. This locus is significantly associated with four taxa in this study (Prevotellaceae, Paraprevotella, ASV7 genus Paraprevotella and Acetatifactor) and overlaps with associations for Clostridiales, Clostridiaceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Deferribacteriaceae (Snijders et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide association mapping results and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Identifying significant overlap in the identification of host loci with previous studies suggests that some of the same genes and/or mechanisms influencing major members of gut microbial communities are conserved even in the face of community 'reset' in the context of rederivation.
source: As previous studies were based on rederived mouse strains, identifying significant overlap in the identification of host loci suggests that some of the same genes and/or mechanisms influencing major members of gut microbial communities are conserved even in the face of community 'reset' in the context of rederivation.
evidence: Inferred from the overlap with previous studies using rederived strains.

claim: The identity of the taxa associated with conserved loci is not always the same across studies, which suggests that functional redundancy may contribute to these observations.
source: The identity of the taxa is however not always the same, which suggests that functional redundancy may contribute to these observations, if, for example, several bacterial taxa fulfill the same function within the gut microbiome (Moya and Ferrer, 2016; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from differences in taxa identity across studies and cited research on functional redundancy.

claim: A limitation of the current and previous genetic studies is that the phenotypes used for mapping are based on relative abundance rather than absolute, quantitative estimates.
source: A limitation of the current and previous genetic studies is that the phenotypes used for mapping are based on relative abundance rather than absolute, quantitative estimates.
evidence: Describes a limitation of the study methodology.

claim: An increase in a given taxon's abundance will necessarily lead to a decrease in abundance among all other taxa when using relative abundance, which can lead to a number of potential biases.
source: Specifically, an increase in a given taxon's abundance will necessarily lead to a decrease in abundance among all other taxa, which can lead to a number of potential biases (Kathagen et al., 2017; Barlow et al., 2020).
evidence: Describes a limitation of relative abundance measurements and cites research on compositional data biases.

claim: 12 of the 14 significantly enriched KEGG pathways were shown to be related to interactions with bacteria.
source: Furthermore, by analysing the functions of the genes closest to significant SNPs, we found that 12 of the 14 significantly enriched KEGG pathways were shown to be related to interactions with bacteria (Fonken et al., 2010 Thaiss et al., 2014; Neumann et al., 2014; Thaiss et al., 2015a; Thaiss et al., 2015b; Castoldi, 2015; Erdman and Poutahidis, 2016; Thaiss et al., 2016; Deaver et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2020; Nagpal et al., 2020; Hollander and Kaunitz, 2019; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis and citations to research on pathway functions.

claim: At the centre of the curated candidate gene network is a set of 22 proteins involved in G-protein coupled receptor signalling.
source: To improve the robustness of our results, we combined multiple lines of evidence to prioritise candidates, resulting in a network of 79 genes (Supplementary file 7). At the centre of this network is a set of 22 proteins involved in G-protein coupled receptor signalling (Figure 6, red nodes).
